modules.exercisesFile:
# Rule-recognition work, saved by the program.
# Format: see data/README.md; the fields are those of the course's recognition-problems.rec.
# The digest on the last line must match the records, or the program refuses the file.

problem: Recog 1.001
argument: P->P . P  .: P
comment: This is a perfectly correct application of MP.  The fact that the rule is stated using distinct antecedent and consequent allows the antecedent and consequent to be distinct, but does not require it.

problem: Recog 1.002
argument: ~T->(T->U) . ~(T->U)  .: ~~T
comment: Note that the conclusion must be as given, and cannot be "T", which is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional.

problem: Recog 1.003
argument: W->X . ~X  .: ~W

problem: Recog 1.004
argument: ~(~P->W)  .: P->W
comment: The premise is the negation of a conditional, not the negation of a negation.  If the premise had been \l"~~(P->W)"\l the conclusion could have been obtained by DN.

problem: Recog 1.005
argument: ~Q->~R . R  .: Q
comment: The second premise is not the negation of the consequent of the conditional (as is required), and the conclusion is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional (as is also required).  The result can be obtained from those two premises, but not directly by a single application of MT.  Rather, one must first apply DN to the second premise, then apply MT to obtain \l"~~Q"\l, then apply a second DN to that result.

problem: Recog 1.006
argument: ~~~Z  .: ~Z

problem: Recog 1.007
argument: (~Q->S)->P . ~Q->S  .: P
comment: Note that the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the second premise, but cannot be dropped in the first premise.

problem: Recog 1.008
argument: ~~P  .: ~~P

problem: Recog 1.009
argument: ~~P->~Q . ~~Q  .: ~P
comment: This case is rather like 1.005.  Although MT can be applied directly to these premises, it yields \l"~~~P"\l rather than \l"~P"\l.  The latter requires an application of DN.

problem: Recog 1.010
argument: T->S  .: ~~(T->S)
comment: As in 1.007, the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the premise, but cannot be dropped in the conclusion.

problem: Recog 1.011
argument: P->Y . ~P  .: ~Y
comment: A wrong way around attempt to apply MT.  To apply MT, the second premise must be the negation of the consequent of the conditional rather than being the negation of the antecedent.

problem: Recog 1.012
argument: ~(R->T)->U . ~~U  .: ~~(R->T)
comment: One too many negations in the second premise.

problem: Recog 1.013
argument: T . T->~Q  .: ~Q
comment: Note that the order in which the premises appear does not matter.

problem: Recog 1.014
argument: ~~~P->Q  .: ~P->Q
comment: If we restore the dropped parentheses, we will see that the premise is \l"(~~~P->Q)"\l, not \l"~~~(P->Q)"\l, and thus a conditional, not a negation.  Perhaps this is an attempt to apply the rule of DN to just the antecedent of the conditional, the \l"~~~P"\l part.  But rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.  (Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)

problem: Recog 1.015
argument: ~(R->~S)->(~P->~T) . ~(~P->~T)  .: ~~(R->~S)

problem: Recog 1.016
argument: P->Y  .: P->Y
comment: One may wonder about the utility of the rule R.  Its most common use is to bring a line required for boxing and canceling down below the Show line that is to be canceled.  In theory, this rule is dispensable, in the sense that any derivation that uses it can be transformed into a derivation that does not use it.

problem: Recog 1.017
argument: (P->Q)->~~S  .: (P->Q)->S
comment: This failed attempt to apply DN violates the Prime Directive:  Rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.

problem: Recog 1.018
argument: ~W . W->X  .: ~X
comment: Another cock-eyed attempt at MT.  Like 1.011, except for the (irrelevant) order of the premises.  If the first premise and the conclusion traded places, it would be a correct application of MT.

problem: Recog 1.019
argument: R->Q  .: ~~R->Q
comment: Compare 1.014.  The premise, in official notation, is \l"(R->Q)"\l; the conclusion is \l"(~~R->Q)"\l.  This is not a correct application of DN.

problem: Recog 1.020
argument: (P->T)->(R->(S->P)) . (P->T) . R  .: S->P
comment: The conclusion can be obtained by two applications of MP, the first to premises 1 and 2, the second to the result and premise 3, but it cannot be obtained by a single application of MP.  Using queuing, a correct justification for the conclusion would read, "PR1 PR2 MP PR3 MP".

problem: Recog 2.001
argument: ~(P&Q)  .: ~Q
comment: This appears to be another attempt to apply an inference rule, here, Simplification, to the interior of a formula (see explanations of answers to problems 1.014 and 1.017 of Chapter I).\nRULES MAY NEVER BE APPLIED TO THE INTERIOR OF A FORMULA.\n(Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)

problem: Recog 2.002
argument: ~(P|Q)&((R->~P)<->S)  .: ~(P|Q)
comment: In Command Mode, one can avoid a query by directly citing the form of the rule, here, Simplification on the left, or SL.

problem: Recog 2.003
argument: ~P&Q->R  .: ~P
comment: The attempt to Simplify reflect an incorrect parsing of the premise, which is correctly parsed as a conditional \l"((~P&Q)->R)"\l not a conjunction.

problem: Recog 2.004
argument: ~S|R . P->Q  .: (P->Q)&(~S|R)
comment: Note that both pairs of parentheses are required in the conclusion; the first by the fact that \l"->"\l is a major connective, the second by the fact that \l"&"\l and \l"|"\l are both minor connectives.

problem: Recog 2.005
argument: ((P->~(Q|~S))|T)&S  .: S
comment: Good parsing!

problem: Recog 2.006
argument: (R|S) . Q<->P  .: (R|S)&Q<->P
comment: This attempt to apply ADJ fails because the conclusion is a biconditional (the major connective as between \l"&"\l and \l"<->"\l).  If the conclusion had been written \l"(R|S)&(Q<->P)"\l, it would have been a correct application of ADJ.

problem: Recog 2.007
argument: ~P . ~(Q<->R)  .: ~(P&(Q<->R))
comment: Perhaps the perpetrator of this argument thought to hold the negations in abeyance while adjoining the negated formulas, then carry down the negation.

problem: Recog 2.008
argument: P->Q  .: P->Q|R
comment: Like 1.006, this attempt at Addition miscarries because of the lack of parentheses in the conclusion.  A correct application of ADD (more precisely ADDR) would yield \l"(P->Q)|R"\l.

problem: Recog 2.009
argument: R&S  .: Q|(R&S)
comment: For this correct application of Addition on the Left using the parameter "Q" for the formula to be added, one could simply enter "PR1 ADDL/Q".  In Command Mode, no queries would result.

problem: Recog 2.010
argument: R->S  .: (R->S)|(S->Q)
comment: As in 2.009, a Command Mode command of \l"PR1 ADDR/(S->Q)"\l would generate the line without queries.  Note that when using parameters, even \l "PR1 ADDR/S->Q"\l will generate the correct line.

problem: Recog 2.011
argument: P&~Q  .: (P|Q)&(~Q|R)
comment: This doesn't begin to be derivable by the application of a single primitive rule.  However, the following single command, queued and with parameters, will generate the line: "PR1 SL ADDR/Q PR1 SR ADDR/R ADJ".

problem: Recog 2.012
argument: P|Q  .: P|Q|R
comment: Note that the conclusion is associated to the left.  Thus, in official notation, \l"((P|Q)|R)"\l.

problem: Recog 2.013
argument: P|Q  .: R|P|Q
comment: As in 2.012, our conventions for dropping parentheses allows them to be dropped for a series of disjuncts only if the disjuncts are associated to the left.  Hence, the conclusion, in official notation, is \l"((R|P)|Q)"\l.  This formula is not directly derivable from \l"(P|Q)"\l by Addition.  Only \l"(R|(P|Q))"\l follows directly by ADD.  In order to get the conclusion as it appears, one must then use the Derived Rule of Assoc (or derive the appropriate instance of T54).

problem: Recog 2.014
argument: ~(R|S)|(P->S) . ~(P->S)  .: ~(R|S)

problem: Recog 2.015
argument: P|~(Q&R) . ~P  .:Q&R
comment: What happened to the negation? This failed attempt at MTP should have had as its conclusion \l"~(Q&R)"\l.

problem: Recog 2.016
argument: P|~(S->(T|R)) . ~P  .: ~(S->(T|R))
comment: Note that MTP applies equally to either the left disjunct or the right disjunct (compare 2.014).

problem: Recog 2.017
argument: (P|Q)->R . ~P  .: Q
comment: One can't just ignore the \l"->R"\l.

problem: Recog 2.018
argument: ~(P<->Q)  .: ~(P->Q)
comment: Shame shame! Again, an attempt to apply BC to the interior of a formula (see 2.001).

problem: Recog 2.019
argument: P|~R<->Q&~S  .: Q&~S->P|~R
comment: Bingo!  This is a correct application of BC in the Right to Left direction.  Either "PR1 BC", which will generate a query about which direction is desired, or "PR1 BCR", which will not generate a query, can be used as justification.

problem: Recog 2.020
argument: P<->Q&R  .: Q->P
comment: That old devil parsing has blinded the perpetrator.  The premise is indeed a biconditional, \l"(P<->(Q&R))"\l, but the BCR would yield \l"Q&R->P"\l, not \l"Q->P"\l.

problem: Recog 2.021
argument: P&Q->R . R->P&Q  .: R<->P&Q
comment: The biconditional in either direction can be derived from these two premises.

problem: Recog 2.022
argument: (P->Q)->R . R->(Q->P)  .: R<->(P<->Q)
comment: This is a sly one.  The \l"(P->Q)"\l gets reversed in the second premise.  The second premise needed to be \l"R->(P->Q)"\l to validly yield any conclusion by CB, and even then it wouldn't yield this conclusion.  (What would it yield?)

problem: Recog 2.023
argument: (S|~R)->R . R->(S|~R)  .: (S|~R)<->R

problem: Recog 3.001
argument: forall x (Fx->Gy)  .: Fx->Gy
comment: The instantial term is the variable "x" itself.  In the conclusion, the outermost parentheses were dropped in accordance with the conventions.

problem: Recog 3.002
argument: exists x Fx  .: Fa
comment: EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "a" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.

problem: Recog 3.003
argument: Gx  .: forall x Gx
comment: There is no inference rule, UG, for universally generalizing a formula.  Instead, we have Universal Derivation (UD) as a new form for boxing & canceling.

problem: Recog 3.004
argument: exists y Gy  .: GA
comment: In EI, the instantial term must be a variable; "A" is a name letter, not a variable.

problem: Recog 3.005
argument: forall x Gy  .: Gy
comment: The quantifier phrase is vacuous; it binds nothing.  You may wonder what the instantial term is.  Let it be any term, say "A". If we replace all the occurrences of "x" that are bound by the vacuous quantifier, then since there are no such occurrences, we change nothing.

problem: Recog 3.006
argument: exists x Gy  .: Gz
comment: As in 3.005, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.  Therefore any application of EI would yield "Gy", not "Gz".

problem: Recog 3.007
argument: forall x exists y (Fx->Gy|Hx)  .: exists y (FA->Gy|HA)
comment: The instantial term is "A".

problem: Recog 3.008
argument: exists x forall y (Fy->Gx)  .: forall y (Fy->Gb)
comment: EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "b" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.

problem: Recog 3.009
argument: FA->GA  .: exists y (FA->Gy)
comment: The instantial term is "A".  Only the second occurrence was generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.

problem: Recog 3.010
argument: exists x Gy  .: Gy
comment: The quantifier phrase is vacuous; so we may assume that the instantial variable is the first variable not occurring in the derivation.  It is always correct to EI or UI vacuous quantifier phrases.

problem: Recog 3.011
argument: FA->GA  .: exists y (Fy->Gy)
comment: As in 3.009, the instantial term is "A".  Here all occurrences were generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.

problem: Recog 3.012
argument: ~forall x exists y (Fz<->Gy)  .: exists z ~exists y (Fz<->Gy)
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply QN, but the rewriting of the variable "x" to "z" prevents this from being a correct application of QN.

problem: Recog 3.013
argument: forall x exists y (Fx->Gy)  .: exists y (Fy->Gy)
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "y" as the instantial term.  But the occurrence of "y" in "Fy" got picked up by the preexisting quantifier phrase \l"!y"\l.  To put it in more formal terms, not all occurrences of "x" that were bound by the initial universal quantifier were replaced by free occurrences of "y".

problem: Recog 3.014
argument: forall x (exists z (Fx&Gy)->exists x Hx|Gx)  .: exists z (FA&Gy)->exists x Hx|Gx
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "A" as the instantial term, but the final occurrence of "x", which is bound by the relevant universal quantifier, was not replaced.

problem: Recog 3.015
argument: exists x (Fx&Gy)  .: Fa&Gy
comment: EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "a" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.

problem: Recog 3.016
argument: FA&exists x (Gx|GA)  .: exists x (Fx&exists x (Gx|Gx))
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to both occurrences of "A" (as the instantial term), and with "x" as the generalized variable, but the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion got picked up by the preexisting internal quantifier phrase \l"!x"\l.

problem: Recog 3.017
argument: FA&exists x (Gx|GA)  .: exists y (Fy&exists x (Gx|Gy))
comment: Compare 3.016.  EG is applied to both occurrences of "A" (as the instantial term), and with "y" as the generalized variable.

problem: Recog 3.018
argument: (forall x Fx->exists y (Hy|Hx))  .: FB->exists y (Hy|HB)
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "B" as the instantial term, but the quantifier phrase \l"@x"\l is not the main connective in the premise, the conditional is, so UI is not applicable. In addition, the universal quantifier phrase does not even bind the final occurrence of "x", which was replaced by "B".

problem: Recog 3.019
argument: forall x (Fx->exists y (FB&Gy))  .: exists z (forall x Fx->exists y (Fz&Gy))
comment: If the first left parenthesis in the premise had been to the left of the initial quantifier, this would have been a correct application of EG, with "B" as the instantial term and "z" as the generalized variable, but as it is, it is nothing.

problem: Recog 3.020
argument: exists z (FA&Gz)->exists x Hx|GA  .:  exists x (exists z (FA&Gz)->exists x Hx|Gx)
comment: Only the second occurrence of "A" (as the instantial term) is generalized on, and with "x" as the generalized variable.  Note that the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion is bound by the initial quantifier phrase since it (the final "x") does not lie within the scope of the inner existential quantifier on "x".

problem: Recog 3.021
argument: exists z (FA&Gy)->exists x Hx|GA  .: exists x (exists z (Fx&Gy)->exists x Hx|Gx)
comment: Exactly like 3.020 except that both occurrences of "A" were generalized on.

problem: Recog 3.022
argument: ~~exists x Fx  .: ~forall x ~Fx
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply QN to the interior of a formula, which is never correct.

problem: Recog 3.023
argument: ~exists x ~GA  .: forall x GA
comment: This is one of the less used forms (QN6, in fact). Also, as it happens, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.

problem: Recog 3.024
argument: ~forall x (Fx|Gx)  .: exists x (~Fx&~Gx)
comment: This is a valid argument, but it cannot be achieved in a single step.  The argument, as given, appears to be a combination of first applying QN to the premise, and then applying one of the DeMorgan laws to the interior of the result.

problem: Recog 3.025
argument: ~exists x ~GA  .: forall x ~~GA
comment: Compare 3.023.  This uses a more familiar form of QN (QN3) than 3.023 does.

problem: Recog 3.026
argument: forall x forall y (Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx)  .: Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx
comment: None, although the result can be achieved by a sequence of two applications of UI, perhaps even queued on a single line.

problem: Recog 3.027
argument: forall x ~Fx  .: ~exists x Fx

problem: Recog 3.028
argument: exists x Fx->FA|forall x Gx  .: exists x (exists x Fx->Fx|forall x Gx)
comment: "\"A\" is the instantial term, and \"x\" is the generalized variable.  Note that the initial existential generalization in the conclusion does not bind any occurrence of \"x\" except the one that replaces \"A\"."

problem: Recog 3.029
argument: exists y forall x (Fx|Gx)  .: forall y exists x (~Fx&~Gx)
comment: The conclusion, in fact, is equivalent to the negation of the premise; it certainly is not a consequence of it.

problem: Recog 3.030
argument: forall x (Fx->exists y (FB&Gy))  .: forall x (Fx->exists z exists y (Fz&Gy))
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to the interior of a formula, in fact, to just the consequent of the inner conditional (with "B" as the instantial term, and "z" as the generalized variable).

problem: Recog 3.031
argument: forall x (exists z Fz->forall z Gz|Fx)  .: forall z (exists z Fz->forall z Gz|Fz)
comment: The generalized variable "x" in the premise is rewritten to "z".  Note that the preexisting occurrences of "z" continue to be bound to the same occurrences of quantifiers.

problem: Recog 3.032
argument: forall x (exists x Fx->forall z (Gz|Fx))  .: forall z (exists x Fx->forall z (Gz|Fz))
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But the final occurrence of a variable ("x" in the premise, "z" in the conclusion) is no longer bound to the initial quantifier phrase.

problem: Recog 3.033
argument: exists x (Fz<->forall z Gz|Fx)  .: exists z (Fz<->forall z Gz|Fz)
comment: This also appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But this time the first occurrence of the variable "z", which is free in the premise, gets picked up by the rewritten initial quantifier phrase.

problem: Recog 4.001
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(zz)
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but there is no way to replace "x" in "A(xyx)" and come out with just "z".

problem: Recog 4.002
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(xyx)z)

problem: Recog 4.003
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(yyy)z)

problem: Recog 4.004
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(xxx)z)
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but replacing the bound variable "x" by "x" would yield "A(xyx)" not "A(xxx)".

problem: Recog 4.005
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(CyB)z)
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but both "B" and "C" have been used to replace "x".  You cannot UI to two different terms at once.

problem: Recog 4.006
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(CyC)z)

problem: Recog 4.007
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(ByB)z)

problem: Recog 4.008
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(A(xyx)yA(xyx))z)

problem: Recog 4.009
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(B(y)yB(y))z)

problem: Recog 4.010
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(B(C(z))yB(C(z)))z)
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but when the bound variable "x" is replaced by "B(C(z))", the free "z" in "B(C(z))" is captured by the "\l!z\l" quantifier.

problem: Recog 4.011
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(C(B(w))yC(B(w)))z)

problem: Recog 4.012
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(wy))

problem: Recog 4.013
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x Fw|G(Cy))
comment: This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the term "A(xB(y))", but this term is bound in the original formula because it contains a bound occurrence of a variable (the "x" is bound by the universal quantifier).  You cannot existentially generalize on a bound term.

problem: Recog 4.014
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xB(w))|G(Cw))

problem: Recog 4.015
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xw)|G(Cy))

problem: Recog 4.016
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists x (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(xy))
comment: Congratulations!  Note that the new initial quantifier, "\l!x\l", does not bind anything in the left disjunct.

problem: Recog 4.017
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists x (forall x FA(xB(x))|G(Cx))
comment: "This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the free \"y\"s, but note that when the first \"y\" is replaced by \"x\", the new occurrence of \"x\" gets captured by the wrong quantifier.  It is bound by the original universal quantifier rather than the newly introduced existential quantifier.  The new occurrences of the variable introduced by an EG must all be bound to the new existential quantifier.  "

problem: Recog 4.018
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists y (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy))

problem: Recog 4.019
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists y (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(yy))
comment: "This looks like an attempt to use EG on \"C\", but in the course of it, the two free occurrences of \"y\" have been picked up. "

problem: Recog 4.020
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists x (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy))
comment: "\"\\l!x\\l\" does not bind anything, but that is okay.  It is a \"vacuous\" quantifier."

problem: Recog 4.021
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xB(y))|Gw)
comment: "This looks like an attempt to use EG, but \"G(Cy)\" cannot be obtained from \"Gw\" by proper substitution.  In the former, \"G\" is a two-place predicate; in the latter it is monadic. "

problem: Recog 5.001
argument: ~exists z G(xzx) . exists z G(yzx) .: x <> y
correct-rules: LL.LL3
comment: This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL3.

problem: Recog 5.002
argument: A(x)=B(y) .: B(y)=A(x)
correct-rules: SM.SM1
comment: This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM1.

problem: Recog 5.003
argument: exists z G(xzx) . y=x .: exists z G(yzy)
correct-rules: LL.LL2
comment: This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL2.  In Command Mode, there would be a query as to which of the (free) occurrences of "x" you wish to replace by "y".  The answer here was "both of them".

problem: Recog 5.004
argument: A(x)<>B(y) .: B(y)<>A(x)
correct-rules: SM.SM2
comment: This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM2.

problem: Recog 5.005
argument: exists x F(xy) . y=x .: exists x F(xx)
correct-rules: none
comment: This looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "y" by "x", but the fact that the replacement gets captured by the quantifier makes it incorrect.

problem: Recog 5.006
argument: A(x)=B(y) .: A(A(x))=A(B(y))
correct-rules: EL
comment: This is a correct application of EL.  The fact that the identity in the premise is between already complex terms only means that you must examine the conclusion more carefully.

problem: Recog 5.007
argument: exists x F(xy) . x=y .: exists x F(yy)
correct-rules: none
comment: Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace "x" by "y", but here the occurrence of the term being replaced, "x", was not free.  This makes the replacement incorrect.

problem: Recog 5.008
argument: A(x)<>B(x) .: C(A(x))<>C(B(x))
correct-rules: none
comment: This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't occur in the form "~D=E .: ~C(D)=C(E)", and would not be valid if it did.  Remember that although ~2=-2 (two is not negative two) the square of 2 is the same number as the square of -2.

problem: Recog 5.009
argument: exists z F(zB(A(x))) . ~exists z F(zB(B(y))) .: A(x)<>B(y)
correct-rules: LL.LL4
comment: This is a correct, though complex, application of LL, in particular of LL4.

problem: Recog 5.010
argument: exists x A(x)=B(x) .: C(A(x)) = C(B(x))
correct-rules: none
comment: This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't allow its premise to occur only as a subformula of another formula.  From the given premise, you could EI to "A(a)=B(a)", and then you could legitimately apply EL to obtain "C(A(a)) = C(B(a))".

problem: Recog 5.011
argument: exists y F(yB(A(x))) . A(x)=B(y) .: exists y F(yB(B(y)))
correct-rules: none
comment: Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "A(x)" by "B(y)", but the fact that this replacement also gets captured by the quantifier makes the inference incorrect.  Remember, a term is bound if it contains a bound occurrence of any variable.

problem: Recog 5.012
argument: A(x)=B(x) .: C(A(x)B(x))=C(B(x)B(x))
correct-rules: EL
comment: This is a correct application of EL.  Here the complex term into which the replacement is being made is "C( __ B(x))", with "C" a 2-place operation symbol, and "B" a 1-place operation symbol.  If you prove T305 to derive EL from LL and SID, you may see more clearly why EL, like LL1, allows you to replace any number of the (free) occurrences of the premise's left-hand term by (free) occurrences of the premise's right-hand term.

modules.workFile:
# Rule-recognition work, saved by the program.
# Format: see data/README.md; the fields are those of the course's recognition-problems.rec.
# The digest on the last line must match the records, or the program refuses the file.

problem: Recog 1.001
argument: P->P . P  .: P
comment: This is a perfectly correct application of MP.  The fact that the rule is stated using distinct antecedent and consequent allows the antecedent and consequent to be distinct, but does not require it.

problem: Recog 1.002
argument: "~T->(T->U) . ~(T->U)  .: ~~T "
comment: Note that the conclusion must be as given, and cannot be "T", which is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional.

problem: Recog 1.003
argument: W->X . ~X  .: ~W
answer: W

problem: Recog 1.005
argument: ~Q->~R . R  .: Q
comment: The second premise is not the negation of the consequent of the conditional (as is required), and the conclusion is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional (as is also required).  The result can be obtained from those two premises, but not directly by a single application of MT.  Rather, one must first apply DN to the second premise, then apply MT to obtain \l"~~Q"\l, then apply a second DN to that result.

problem: Recog 1.006
argument: ~~~Z  .: ~Z

problem: Recog 1.007
argument: "(~Q->S)->P . ~Q->S  .: P "
comment: Note that the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the second premise, but cannot be dropped in the first premise.
answer: W

problem: Recog 1.008
argument: ~~P  .: ~~P

problem: Recog 1.009
argument: ~~P->~Q . ~~Q  .: ~P
comment: This case is rather like 1.005.  Although MT can be applied directly to these premises, it yields \l"~~~P"\l rather than \l"~P"\l.  The latter requires an application of DN.

problem: Recog 1.010
argument: T->S  .: ~~(T->S)
comment: As in 1.007, the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the premise, but cannot be dropped in the conclusion.

problem: Recog 1.012
argument: "~(R->T)->U . ~~U  .: ~~(R->T) "
comment: One too many negations in the second premise.

problem: Recog 1.013
argument: T . T->~Q  .: ~Q
comment: Note that the order in which the premises appear does not matter.

problem: Recog 1.014
argument: ~~~P->Q  .: ~P->Q
comment: If we restore the dropped parentheses, we will see that the premise is \l"(~~~P->Q)"\l, not \l"~~~(P->Q)"\l, and thus a conditional, not a negation.  Perhaps this is an attempt to apply the rule of DN to just the antecedent of the conditional, the \l"~~~P"\l part.  But rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.  (Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)

problem: Recog 1.015
argument: ~(R->~S)->(~P->~T) . ~(~P->~T)  .: ~~(R->~S)
answer: W

problem: Recog 1.016
argument: P->Y  .: P->Y
comment: One may wonder about the utility of the rule R.  Its most common use is to bring a line required for boxing and canceling down below the Show line that is to be canceled.  In theory, this rule is dispensable, in the sense that any derivation that uses it can be transformed into a derivation that does not use it.

problem: Recog 1.017
argument: "(P->Q)->~~S  .: (P->Q)->S "
comment: This failed attempt to apply DN violates the Prime Directive:  Rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.

problem: Recog 1.019
argument: R->Q  .: ~~R->Q
comment: Compare 1.014.  The premise, in official notation, is \l"(R->Q)"\l; the conclusion is \l"(~~R->Q)"\l.  This is not a correct application of DN.
answer: W

problem: Recog 1.020
argument: (P->T)->(R->(S->P)) . (P->T) . R  .: S->P
comment: The conclusion can be obtained by two applications of MP, the first to premises 1 and 2, the second to the result and premise 3, but it cannot be obtained by a single application of MP.  Using queuing, a correct justification for the conclusion would read, "PR1 PR2 MP PR3 MP".

problem: Recog 2.001
argument: ~(P&Q)  .: ~Q
comment: This appears to be another attempt to apply an inference rule, here, Simplification, to the interior of a formula (see explanations of answers to problems 1.014 and 1.017 of Chapter I).\nRULES MAY NEVER BE APPLIED TO THE INTERIOR OF A FORMULA.\n(Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)

problem: Recog 2.002
argument: "~(P|Q)&((R->~P)<->S)  .: ~(P|Q) "
comment: In Command Mode, one can avoid a query by directly citing the form of the rule, here, Simplification on the left, or SL.

problem: Recog 2.003
argument: ~P&Q->R  .: ~P
comment: The attempt to Simplify reflect an incorrect parsing of the premise, which is correctly parsed as a conditional \l"((~P&Q)->R)"\l not a conjunction.
answer: W

problem: Recog 2.004
argument: ~S|R . P->Q  .: (P->Q)&(~S|R)
comment: Note that both pairs of parentheses are required in the conclusion; the first by the fact that \l"->"\l is a major connective, the second by the fact that \l"&"\l and \l"|"\l are both minor connectives.

problem: Recog 2.006
argument: (R|S) . Q<->P  .: (R|S)&Q<->P
comment: This attempt to apply ADJ fails because the conclusion is a biconditional (the major connective as between \l"&"\l and \l"<->"\l).  If the conclusion had been written \l"(R|S)&(Q<->P)"\l, it would have been a correct application of ADJ.

problem: Recog 2.007
argument: "~P . ~(Q<->R)  .: ~(P&(Q<->R)) "
comment: Perhaps the perpetrator of this argument thought to hold the negations in abeyance while adjoining the negated formulas, then carry down the negation.
answer: W

problem: Recog 2.008
argument: P->Q  .: P->Q|R
comment: Like 1.006, this attempt at Addition miscarries because of the lack of parentheses in the conclusion.  A correct application of ADD (more precisely ADDR) would yield \l"(P->Q)|R"\l.

problem: Recog 2.009
argument: R&S  .: Q|(R&S)
comment: For this correct application of Addition on the Left using the parameter "Q" for the formula to be added, one could simply enter "PR1 ADDL/Q".  In Command Mode, no queries would result.

problem: Recog 2.010
argument: R->S  .: (R->S)|(S->Q)
comment: As in 2.009, a Command Mode command of \l"PR1 ADDR/(S->Q)"\l would generate the line without queries.  Note that when using parameters, even \l "PR1 ADDR/S->Q"\l will generate the correct line.

problem: Recog 2.011
argument: P&~Q  .: (P|Q)&(~Q|R)
comment: This doesn't begin to be derivable by the application of a single primitive rule.  However, the following single command, queued and with parameters, will generate the line: "PR1 SL ADDR/Q PR1 SR ADDR/R ADJ".
answer: W

problem: Recog 2.013
argument: P|Q  .: R|P|Q
comment: As in 2.012, our conventions for dropping parentheses allows them to be dropped for a series of disjuncts only if the disjuncts are associated to the left.  Hence, the conclusion, in official notation, is \l"((R|P)|Q)"\l.  This formula is not directly derivable from \l"(P|Q)"\l by Addition.  Only \l"(R|(P|Q))"\l follows directly by ADD.  In order to get the conclusion as it appears, one must then use the Derived Rule of Assoc (or derive the appropriate instance of T54).

problem: Recog 2.014
argument: ~(R|S)|(P->S) . ~(P->S)  .: ~(R|S)

problem: Recog 2.015
argument: P|~(Q&R) . ~P  .:Q&R
comment: What happened to the negation? This failed attempt at MTP should have had as its conclusion \l"~(Q&R)"\l.
answer: W

problem: Recog 2.016
argument: P|~(S->(T|R)) . ~P  .: ~(S->(T|R))
comment: Note that MTP applies equally to either the left disjunct or the right disjunct (compare 2.014).

problem: Recog 2.017
argument: "(P|Q)->R . ~P  .: Q "
comment: One can't just ignore the \l"->R"\l.

problem: Recog 2.018
argument: ~(P<->Q)  .: ~(P->Q)
comment: Shame shame! Again, an attempt to apply BC to the interior of a formula (see 2.001).

problem: Recog 2.020
argument: P<->Q&R  .: Q->P
comment: That old devil parsing has blinded the perpetrator.  The premise is indeed a biconditional, \l"(P<->(Q&R))"\l, but the BCR would yield \l"Q&R->P"\l, not \l"Q->P"\l.

problem: Recog 2.021
argument: P&Q->R . R->P&Q  .: R<->P&Q
comment: The biconditional in either direction can be derived from these two premises.

problem: Recog 2.022
argument: "(P->Q)->R . R->(Q->P)  .: R<->(P<->Q) "
comment: This is a sly one.  The \l"(P->Q)"\l gets reversed in the second premise.  The second premise needed to be \l"R->(P->Q)"\l to validly yield any conclusion by CB, and even then it wouldn't yield this conclusion.  (What would it yield?)

problem: Recog 2.023
argument: (S|~R)->R . R->(S|~R)  .: (S|~R)<->R
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.001
argument: forall x (Fx->Gy)  .: Fx->Gy
comment: The instantial term is the variable "x" itself.  In the conclusion, the outermost parentheses were dropped in accordance with the conventions.

problem: Recog 3.002
argument: exists x Fx  .: Fa
comment: EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "a" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.

problem: Recog 3.004
argument: "exists y Gy  .: GA "
comment: In EI, the instantial term must be a variable; "A" is a name letter, not a variable.
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.005
argument: forall x Gy  .: Gy
comment: The quantifier phrase is vacuous; it binds nothing.  You may wonder what the instantial term is.  Let it be any term, say "A". If we replace all the occurrences of "x" that are bound by the vacuous quantifier, then since there are no such occurrences, we change nothing.

problem: Recog 3.006
argument: exists x Gy  .: Gz
comment: As in 3.005, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.  Therefore any application of EI would yield "Gy", not "Gz".

problem: Recog 3.007
argument: forall x exists y (Fx->Gy|Hx)  .: exists y (FA->Gy|HA)
comment: The instantial term is "A".

problem: Recog 3.008
argument: exists x forall y (Fy->Gx)  .: forall y (Fy->Gb)
comment: EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "b" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.009
argument: "FA->GA  .: exists y (FA->Gy) "
comment: The instantial term is "A".  Only the second occurrence was generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.

problem: Recog 3.011
argument: FA->GA  .: exists y (Fy->Gy)
comment: As in 3.009, the instantial term is "A".  Here all occurrences were generalized on.  In the premise, the outermost parentheses were dropped, but they were restored, as is required, in the conclusion.

problem: Recog 3.012
argument: ~forall x exists y (Fz<->Gy)  .: exists z ~exists y (Fz<->Gy)
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply QN, but the rewriting of the variable "x" to "z" prevents this from being a correct application of QN.
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.013
argument: forall x exists y (Fx->Gy)  .: exists y (Fy->Gy)
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "y" as the instantial term.  But the occurrence of "y" in "Fy" got picked up by the preexisting quantifier phrase \l"!y"\l.  To put it in more formal terms, not all occurrences of "x" that were bound by the initial universal quantifier were replaced by free occurrences of "y".

problem: Recog 3.014
argument: "forall x (exists z (Fx&Gy)->exists x Hx|Gx)  .: exists z (FA&Gy)->exists x Hx|Gx "
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "A" as the instantial term, but the final occurrence of "x", which is bound by the relevant universal quantifier, was not replaced.

problem: Recog 3.015
argument: exists x (Fx&Gy)  .: Fa&Gy
comment: EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "a" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.

problem: Recog 3.016
argument: FA&exists x (Gx|GA)  .: exists x (Fx&exists x (Gx|Gx))
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to both occurrences of "A" (as the instantial term), and with "x" as the generalized variable, but the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion got picked up by the preexisting internal quantifier phrase \l"!x"\l.
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.018
argument: (forall x Fx->exists y (Hy|Hx))  .: FB->exists y (Hy|HB)
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply UI, with "B" as the instantial term, but the quantifier phrase \l"@x"\l is not the main connective in the premise, the conditional is, so UI is not applicable. In addition, the universal quantifier phrase does not even bind the final occurrence of "x", which was replaced by "B".

problem: Recog 3.019
argument: "forall x (Fx->exists y (FB&Gy))  .: exists z (forall x Fx->exists y (Fz&Gy)) "
comment: If the first left parenthesis in the premise had been to the left of the initial quantifier, this would have been a correct application of EG, with "B" as the instantial term and "z" as the generalized variable, but as it is, it is nothing.

problem: Recog 3.020
argument: exists z (FA&Gz)->exists x Hx|GA  .:  exists x (exists z (FA&Gz)->exists x Hx|Gx)
comment: Only the second occurrence of "A" (as the instantial term) is generalized on, and with "x" as the generalized variable.  Note that the final occurrence of "x" in the conclusion is bound by the initial quantifier phrase since it (the final "x") does not lie within the scope of the inner existential quantifier on "x".
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.021
argument: exists z (FA&Gy)->exists x Hx|GA  .: exists x (exists z (Fx&Gy)->exists x Hx|Gx)
comment: Exactly like 3.020 except that both occurrences of "A" were generalized on.

problem: Recog 3.022
argument: ~~exists x Fx  .: ~forall x ~Fx
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply QN to the interior of a formula, which is never correct.

problem: Recog 3.023
argument: ~exists x ~GA  .: forall x GA
comment: This is one of the less used forms (QN6, in fact). Also, as it happens, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.

problem: Recog 3.025
argument: ~exists x ~GA  .: forall x ~~GA
comment: Compare 3.023.  This uses a more familiar form of QN (QN3) than 3.023 does.

problem: Recog 3.026
argument: forall x forall y (Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx)  .: Fx&Gy<->Gy&Fx
comment: None, although the result can be achieved by a sequence of two applications of UI, perhaps even queued on a single line.

problem: Recog 3.027
argument: forall x ~Fx  .: ~exists x Fx

problem: Recog 3.028
argument: exists x Fx->FA|forall x Gx  .: exists x (exists x Fx->Fx|forall x Gx)
comment: "\"A\" is the instantial term, and \"x\" is the generalized variable.  Note that the initial existential generalization in the conclusion does not bind any occurrence of \"x\" except the one that replaces \"A\"."
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.029
argument: "exists y forall x (Fx|Gx)  .: forall y exists x (~Fx&~Gx) "
comment: The conclusion, in fact, is equivalent to the negation of the premise; it certainly is not a consequence of it.

problem: Recog 3.030
argument: forall x (Fx->exists y (FB&Gy))  .: forall x (Fx->exists z exists y (Fz&Gy))
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply EG to the interior of a formula, in fact, to just the consequent of the inner conditional (with "B" as the instantial term, and "z" as the generalized variable).

problem: Recog 3.032
argument: forall x (exists x Fx->forall z (Gz|Fx))  .: forall z (exists x Fx->forall z (Gz|Fz))
comment: This appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But the final occurrence of a variable ("x" in the premise, "z" in the conclusion) is no longer bound to the initial quantifier phrase.
answer: W

problem: Recog 3.033
argument: exists x (Fz<->forall z Gz|Fx)  .: exists z (Fz<->forall z Gz|Fz)
comment: This also appears to be an attempt to apply AV by rewriting the generalized variable "x" in the premise to "z".  But this time the first occurrence of the variable "z", which is free in the premise, gets picked up by the rewritten initial quantifier phrase.

problem: Recog 4.001
argument: "forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(zz) "
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but there is no way to replace "x" in "A(xyx)" and come out with just "z".

problem: Recog 4.002
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(xyx)z)

problem: Recog 4.003
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(yyy)z)
answer: W

problem: Recog 4.004
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(xxx)z)
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but replacing the bound variable "x" by "x" would yield "A(xyx)" not "A(xxx)".

problem: Recog 4.006
argument: "forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(CyC)z) "

problem: Recog 4.007
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(ByB)z)
answer: W

problem: Recog 4.008
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(A(xyx)yA(xyx))z)

problem: Recog 4.009
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(B(y)yB(y))z)

problem: Recog 4.010
argument: forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(B(C(z))yB(C(z)))z)
comment: This looks like an attempt to use UI, but when the bound variable "x" is replaced by "B(C(z))", the free "z" in "B(C(z))" is captured by the "\l!z\l" quantifier.

problem: Recog 4.011
argument: "forall x exists z F(A(xyx)z)  .: exists z F(A(C(B(w))yC(B(w)))z) "
answer: W

problem: Recog 4.013
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x Fw|G(Cy))
comment: This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the term "A(xB(y))", but this term is bound in the original formula because it contains a bound occurrence of a variable (the "x" is bound by the universal quantifier).  You cannot existentially generalize on a bound term.

problem: Recog 4.014
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xB(w))|G(Cw))

problem: Recog 4.015
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xw)|G(Cy))
answer: W

problem: Recog 4.016
argument: "forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists x (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(xy)) "
comment: Congratulations!  Note that the new initial quantifier, "\l!x\l", does not bind anything in the left disjunct.

problem: Recog 4.017
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists x (forall x FA(xB(x))|G(Cx))
comment: "This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the free \"y\"s, but note that when the first \"y\" is replaced by \"x\", the new occurrence of \"x\" gets captured by the wrong quantifier.  It is bound by the original universal quantifier rather than the newly introduced existential quantifier.  The new occurrences of the variable introduced by an EG must all be bound to the new existential quantifier.  "

problem: Recog 4.018
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists y (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy))

problem: Recog 4.020
argument: forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists x (forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy))
comment: "\"\\l!x\\l\" does not bind anything, but that is okay.  It is a \"vacuous\" quantifier."

problem: Recog 4.021
argument: "forall x FA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: exists w (forall x FA(xB(y))|Gw) "
comment: "This looks like an attempt to use EG, but \"G(Cy)\" cannot be obtained from \"Gw\" by proper substitution.  In the former, \"G\" is a two-place predicate; in the latter it is monadic. "

problem: Recog 5.001
argument: ~exists z G(xzx) . exists z G(yzx) .: x <> y
correct-rules: LL.LL3
comment: This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL3.

problem: Recog 5.002
argument: A(x)=B(y) .: B(y)=A(x)
correct-rules: SM.SM1
comment: This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM1.
answer: W

problem: Recog 5.003
argument: exists z G(xzx) . y=x .: exists z G(yzy)
correct-rules: LL.LL2
comment: This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL2.  In Command Mode, there would be a query as to which of the (free) occurrences of "x" you wish to replace by "y".  The answer here was "both of them".

problem: Recog 5.004
argument: A(x)<>B(y) .: B(y)<>A(x)
correct-rules: SM.SM2
comment: This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM2.

problem: Recog 5.006
argument: A(x)=B(y) .: A(A(x))=A(B(y))
correct-rules: EL
comment: This is a correct application of EL.  The fact that the identity in the premise is between already complex terms only means that you must examine the conclusion more carefully.
answer: W

problem: Recog 5.007
argument: exists x F(xy) . x=y .: exists x F(yy)
correct-rules: none
comment: Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace "x" by "y", but here the occurrence of the term being replaced, "x", was not free.  This makes the replacement incorrect.

problem: Recog 5.008
argument: A(x)<>B(x) .: C(A(x))<>C(B(x))
correct-rules: none
comment: This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't occur in the form "~D=E .: ~C(D)=C(E)", and would not be valid if it did.  Remember that although ~2=-2 (two is not negative two) the square of 2 is the same number as the square of -2.

problem: Recog 5.009
argument: exists z F(zB(A(x))) . ~exists z F(zB(B(y))) .: A(x)<>B(y)
correct-rules: LL.LL4
comment: This is a correct, though complex, application of LL, in particular of LL4.

problem: Recog 5.010
argument: "exists x A(x)=B(x) .: C(A(x)) = C(B(x)) "
correct-rules: none
comment: This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't allow its premise to occur only as a subformula of another formula.  From the given premise, you could EI to "A(a)=B(a)", and then you could legitimately apply EL to obtain "C(A(a)) = C(B(a))".
answer: W

problem: Recog 5.011
argument: exists y F(yB(A(x))) . A(x)=B(y) .: exists y F(yB(B(y)))
correct-rules: none
comment: Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "A(x)" by "B(y)", but the fact that this replacement also gets captured by the quantifier makes the inference incorrect.  Remember, a term is bound if it contains a bound occurrence of any variable.

Recog 4.010`$@x!zF(A(xyx)z)  .: !zF(A(B(C(z))yB(C(z)))z)`=This looks like an attempt to use UI, but when the bound variable "x" is replaced by "B(C(z))", the free "z" in "B(C(z))" is captured by the "\l!z\l" quantifier.`&
Recog 4.011`$@x!zF(A(xyx)z)  .: !zF(A(C(B(w))yC(B(w)))z) `=W`*
Recog 4.013`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !w(@xFw|G(Cy))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the term "A(xB(y))", but this term is bound in the original formula because it contains a bound occurrence of a variable (the "x" is bound by the universal quantifier). Recog 4.014`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !w(@xFA(xB(w))|G(Cw))`=
Recog 4.015`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !w(@xFA(xw)|G(Cy))`=W`*
Recog 4.016`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !x(@xFA(xB(y))|G(xy)) `=Congratulations!  Note that the new initial quantifier, "\l!x\l", does not bind anything in the left disjunct.`&
Recog 4.017`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !x(@xFA(xB(x))|G(Cx))`=This looks like an attempt to use EG by generalizing on the free "y"s, but note that when the first "y" is replaced by "x", the new occurrence of "x" gets captured by the wrong quantifier.  It is bound by the original universal quantifier rather than the newly introduced existential quantifier.  The new occurrences of the variable introduced by an EG must all be bound to the new existential quantifier.  `&
Recog 4.018`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !y(@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy))`=
Recog 4.020`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !x(@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy))`="\l!x\l" does not bind anything, but that is okay.  It is a "vacuous" quantifier.`&
Recog 4.021`$@xFA(xB(y))|G(Cy)  .: !w(@xFA(xB(y))|Gw) `=This looks like an attempt to use EG, but "G(Cy)" cannot be obtained from "Gw" by proper substitution.  In the former, "G" is a two-place predicate; in the latter it is monadic. `&

Recog 5.002`$A(x)=B(y) .: B(y)=A(x)`=SM.SM1`@This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM1.`&W`*
Recog 5.003`$!zG(xzx) . y=x .: !zG(yzy)`=LL.LL2`@This is a correct application of LL, in particular of LL2.  In Command Mode, there would be a query as to which of the (free) occurrences of "x" you wish to replace by "y".  The answer here was "both of them".`&
Recog 5.004`$A(x)<>B(y) .: B(y)<>A(x)`=SM.SM2`@This is a correct application of SM, in particular of SM2.`&
Recog 5.006`$A(x)=B(y) .: A(A(x))=A(B(y))`=EL`@This is a correct application of EL.  The fact that the identity in the premise is between already complex terms only means that you must examine the conclusion more carefully.`&W`*
Recog 5.007`$!xF(xy) . x=y .: !xF(yy)`=none`@Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace "x" by "y", but here the occurrence of the term being replaced, "x", was not free.  This makes the replacement incorrect.`&
Recog 5.008`$A(x)<>B(x) .: C(A(x))<>C(B(x))`=none`@This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't occur in the form "~D=E .: ~C(D)=C(E)", and would not be valid if it did.  Remember that although ~2=-2 (two is not negative two) the square of 2 is the same number as the square of -2.`&
Recog 5.009`$!zF(zB(A(x))) . ~!zF(zB(B(y))) .: A(x)<>B(y)`=LL.LL4`@This is a correct, though complex, application of LL, in particular of LL4.`&
Recog 5.010`$!xA(x)=B(x) .: C(A(x)) = C(B(x)) `=none`@This looks like an attempt to use EL.  But EL doesn't allow its premise to occur only as a subformula of another formula.  From the given premise, you could EI to "A(a)=B(a)", and then you could legitimately apply EL to obtain "C(A(a)) = C(B(a))".`&W`*
Recog 5.011`$!yF(yB(A(x))) . A(x)=B(y) .: !yF(yB(B(y)))`=none`@Like 5.005, this looks like an attempt to use LL to replace the free "A(x)" by "B(y)", but the fact that this replacement also gets captured by the quantifier makes the inference incorrect.  Remember, a term is bound if it contains a bound occurrence of any variable.`&
